Setext-style headings accept an underline that mixes `=` and `-`. A line followed by an underline such as `=-` or `-=-=` is rendered as a heading. A Setext underline has to be made only of `=` (for `

`) or only of `-` (for `

`); a mixed underline should leave both lines as an ordinary paragraph. For example This is not an H1 =- should render as `

This is not an H1\n=-

`, but today it becomes a heading.

Inline raw HTML is not recognised when a quoted attribute value contains `<` or `>`. HTML allows angle brackets inside quoted attribute values, but this input Anything is not passed through as raw HTML. It should render unchanged inside a paragraph:

Anything

Slicing a `numeric_range` with a negative step and no start or stop gives an empty range.

`list(numeric_range(0, 10, 2)[::-1])` is `[]`, although `list(reversed(numeric_range(0, 10, 2)))` is `[8, 6, 4, 2, 0]`, and the two should agree. With a negative step, an omitted start should mean the last element and an omitted stop should mean just past the first element, as with built-in `range` slicing.

`one()` and `only()` ignore a custom exception that is falsy.

If `too_long=` or `too_short=` is given an exception instance whose `__bool__` returns `False`, the functions raise their default `ValueError` instead of the exception you passed. Any exception you pass, falsy or not, should be the one raised.

Also, when a custom `too_long` is given, the default error message should not be built at all: building it calls `repr()` on the first items, which can be slow or can itself raise.

`tomli.loads()` given something other than a `str` fails with a confusing `AttributeError` from inside the parser.

Passing bytes (`tomli.loads(b"v = 1")`) or another type (`tomli.loads(False)`) should raise a `TypeError` with the message `Expected str object, not '<type name>'`, for example `Expected str object, not 'bytes'` and `Expected str object, not 'bool'`.

The pure-Python decoder reports the wrong character and position for a literal control character that follows other text inside a string.

`simplejson.loads('"d\x18"')` raises `JSONDecodeError: Invalid control character 'd' at: line 1 column 2 (char 1)`. It names the first character of the string's content and its position. It should name the control character and point at it: `Invalid control character '\x18' at: line 1 column 3 (char 2)`.

`idna.encode()` and `idna.decode()` leak a raw `TypeError` for input that is not text or bytes.

Both functions are documented to raise `idna.IDNAError` on bad input. Values that are not `str`, `bytes` or bytes-like (for example `42`, `None`, `1.5`, `["a", "b"]` or `{"a": 1}`) should raise `IDNAError` too, instead of a bare `TypeError`.

A `<` comparator with the minor or patch left out matches prereleases it should exclude.

`VersionReq::parse(">1.0.0-alpha, <1.0")` matches `1.0.0-beta`, and so does `>1.0.0-alpha, <1`. Both should not: `<1.0` and `<1` mean below every 1.0.0 version, including its prereleases. Written out in full, `>1.0.0-alpha, <1.0.0` should keep matching `1.0.0-beta` as it does now.

`parse_duration` panics instead of returning an error when nanoseconds carry over into a seconds value that is already at the maximum.

`parse_duration(&format!("{}s1000ms", u64::MAX))` should return `Err(DurationError::NumberOverflow)`, but it panics. The same goes for `format!("{}s 999999999ns 1ns", u64::MAX)`. Carries that fit must still add up: `"1s 999999999ns 1ns"` is exactly 2 seconds.

`BStr`'s `Debug` output escapes some ASCII control characters differently from the rest.

Bytes `\x1a` through `\x1f` come out as Unicode escapes (`\u{1a}` ... `\u{1f}`) while the other control characters use hex escapes (`\x01`, `\x19`, `\x7f`). All of them should use the `\xNN` form, so `format!("{:?}", b"\x19\x1a\x1f".as_bstr())` should be `"\x19\x1a\x1f"`. Tab and newline keep their short forms `\t` and `\n`.
